headline: The yearly defense law sets military funding levels, troop numbers, pay and benefits, and many rules for the Pentagon and other agencies for 2024.
what_it_does: This law authorizes spending for the Defense Department, military construction, and nuclear weapons programs at the Energy Department for fiscal year 2024, and sets the maximum size of each military branch. It changes military pay, housing allowances, health care, and family benefits, and sets new rules on recruiting, buying weapons, and contracts with companies tied to China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea. It also includes many non-defense measures, such as State Department and intelligence agency policies, limits on federal purchases of certain foreign-made drones, and a short extension of a foreign surveillance law through April 19, 2024.

who_it_affects.how: They may get changes to pay and allowances, such as a family separation allowance of up to $400 a month, possible exclusion of housing pay when checking eligibility for the Basic Needs Allowance, and new size and quality standards for barracks.
Some get paid parental leave for up to 12 drill periods after a birth or adoption, and surviving family members can keep TRICARE Reserve Select for three years instead of six months.
The Defense Department may waive cost-sharing for the first three outpatient mental health visits each year, and children of certain military retirees can get hearing aids.

who_it_affects.group: Service members discharged for refusing the COVID-19 vaccine
who_it_affects.how: They can ask to be reinstated within two years of separation and can have their discharge characterization reviewed.

who_it_affects.group: High schools and colleges receiving certain federal funds
who_it_affects.how: They must give military recruiters student contact information within 60 days of a request, and high schools must let recruiters attend career fairs.
Spouses who lose a job because of a military move can defer certain student loans for 180 days, and the law expands help with relicensing costs and job credentials.

who_it_affects.group: Parents of students in Defense Department schools
who_it_affects.how: They gain rights to review curriculum and instructional materials and to meet with teachers at least twice a year.

who_it_affects.group: Small businesses owned by service-disabled veterans
who_it_affects.how: They must get certified by the Small Business Administration to win federal contracts set aside for them, and the government-wide contracting goal for them rises to 5%.
They face new limits on buying from Chinese, Russian, and other foreign sources, rising U.S.-made content requirements, and a one-year pause on any required greenhouse gas reporting.
They are generally barred from buying, and later from using with federal funds, drones made by certain foreign companies, including Chinese-controlled ones, with some exceptions.

who_it_affects.group: Federal workers who responded at the Pentagon and Shanksville after 9/11
who_it_affects.how: They become eligible for the World Trade Center Health Program.

who_it_affects.group: Border Patrol agents at grade GS-12
who_it_affects.how: They can receive an additional overtime payment for certain overtime hours.

who_it_affects.group: Intelligence community employees and their families
who_it_affects.how: They become eligible for in-state tuition at public colleges in the state where they live or are stationed.

when_it_takes_effect: Enacted December 22, 2023; most provisions apply to fiscal year 2024, with some having later dates (for example, the battery purchasing ban begins in FY2027 and the drone use ban begins two years after enactment).
